body_html:
The best Spanish grammar books do two things well: they explain a rule clearly, and they make you practice it until you stop thinking about it. I have worked through every book on this list, first as a learner and later as a translator who still checks grammar every week, and each one earns its place for a different reason. Below are my picks by level, from the first workbook a beginner should buy to the reference grammar I keep on my own desk.

Quick answer
  • Best for beginners: Complete Spanish Step-by-Step
  • Best workbook: Practice Makes Perfect: Complete Spanish Grammar
  • Best for verbs: 501 Spanish Verbs and Practice Makes Perfect: Spanish Verb Tenses
  • Best all-Spanish grammar: Gramática de uso del español
  • Best reference: A New Reference Grammar of Modern Spanish
{{toc}}

For beginners

1. Complete Spanish Step-by-Step

Best for: beginners who want grammar in a clear, logical order · Level: A1–B1

Barbara Bregstein’s book combines a beginner and an intermediate course in one volume. Each chapter adds one grammar point, explains it in plain English and gives you exercises and readings that recycle everything you have learned so far. If grammar has always felt like a list of disconnected rules, this book connects them.

What to know: it is long, and that is a strength. Work through it slowly, a chapter a week. If you want something lighter to start, Easy Spanish Step-by-Step covers the first half; I review it in my list of the {{link:best-books-to-learn-spanish|best books to learn Spanish}}.

See it on Amazon →

2. English Grammar for Students of Spanish

Best for: learners who never studied grammar in English · Level: A1–B1

This small book explains grammar terms like “direct object”, “subjunctive” or “reflexive” using English examples first, then shows how Spanish handles the same idea. Many learners struggle not with Spanish, but with the vocabulary of grammar itself. This book fixes that, and it makes every other grammar book easier to use.

What to know: it is not a course and has few exercises. Think of it as a companion.

See it on Amazon →

Workbooks: where grammar becomes automatic

3. Practice Makes Perfect: Complete Spanish Grammar

Best for: learners who need lots of practice · Level: A2–B1

Gilda Nissenberg’s workbook is the one I recommend most. Every chapter has a short explanation followed by many exercises, from fill-in-the-blank to translation, with an answer key. It covers the present tense, the past tenses, object pronouns, the subjunctive and much more. Doing ten minutes a day from this book will do more for your accuracy than reading about grammar for an hour.

What to know: the explanations are brief; use it with a course book or a teacher.

See it on Amazon →

4. Practice Makes Perfect: Spanish Verb Tenses

Best for: mastering the tenses one by one · Level: A2–B2

Dorothy Richmond’s workbook focuses on verbs, which is where most Spanish mistakes live. It takes each tense in turn, explains when to use it and drills it with plenty of exercises. It is especially good for the classic problem areas: {{link:preterite-vs-imperfect|preterite vs imperfect}} and {{link:indicative-vs-subjunctive|indicative vs subjunctive}}.

What to know: it assumes you know basic present-tense verbs already.

See it on Amazon →

{{image:2}}

For verbs

5. 501 Spanish Verbs

Best for: looking up any conjugation quickly · Level: All levels

This is a reference, not a course: 501 common verbs, each fully conjugated in every tense on one page, with example sentences and common expressions. It is the book I used to keep open while writing, and it is still faster than searching online when you want to see a whole verb at once.

What to know: it won’t teach you when to use each tense. Pair it with a workbook. Online, the conjugation tables on SpanishDict do a similar job; see my list of the {{link:best-spanish-dictionary|best Spanish dictionaries}}.

See it on Amazon →

For learners who want grammar in Spanish

6. Gramática de uso del español

Best for: intermediate learners ready to study in Spanish · Level: A1–C2 (three volumes)

This series, published in Spain, comes in three levels: A1–A2, B1–B2 and C1–C2. Each unit has a page of explanation in simple Spanish and a page of exercises. Studying grammar in Spanish feels hard at first, but it pushes you to think in the language, and the explanations are excellent.

What to know: the examples use Spain Spanish, including vosotros. If you are learning Latin American Spanish, simply skip those forms; see {{link:latin-american-vs-spain-spanish|Latin American vs Spain Spanish}}.

See it on Amazon →

Advanced reference

7. A New Reference Grammar of Modern Spanish

Best for: answering any grammar question in depth · Level: B2–C2

John Butt and Carmen Benjamin’s reference grammar is the book on my desk. It describes Spanish as it is really written and spoken in Spain and Latin America, with real examples and clear notes on regional differences. When a translation raises a question I can’t answer, this is where I look first.

What to know: it is a reference, not a course, and it is too detailed for beginners. Its companion workbook is below. For free, authoritative answers online, the Real Academia Española’s Diccionario panhispánico de dudas is excellent.

See it on Amazon →

8. Practising Spanish Grammar

Best for: advanced learners who want challenging exercises · Level: B2–C2

The companion workbook to the reference grammar above follows the same structure, so you can read a chapter and then practice it. The exercises are demanding and realistic, which is exactly what advanced learners need. Its publisher describes it as usable on its own or alongside the reference grammar; details are on the Routledge page.

What to know: it will feel hard below B2, and that is by design.

See it on Amazon →

{{image:3}}

How to use a grammar book without getting bored

  1. Do a little every day. Ten minutes of exercises daily beats two hours on Sunday.
  2. Write your own sentences. After each exercise, write three sentences about your life using the same rule.
  3. Read and listen alongside. Grammar sticks when you meet it in real Spanish. Bilingual books and podcasts help; see the {{link:best-spanish-podcasts|best Spanish podcasts}}.
  4. Go back to your mistakes. Mark the exercises you get wrong and redo them a week later. My guide to {{link:common-spanish-mistakes|common Spanish mistakes}} shows the errors most learners repeat.

Which grammar book should you buy first?

If you are a beginner, start with Complete Spanish Step-by-Step and add Practice Makes Perfect for exercises. If you are intermediate, add the verb tenses workbook and try one volume of Gramática de uso del español. Keep 501 Spanish Verbs nearby at every level. Save the reference grammar for when your questions get too detailed for the others; you will know when that happens.

{{if:best-spanish-youtube-channels}}

When you want grammar explained on video, the {{link:best-spanish-youtube-channels|best Spanish YouTube channels}} list includes three good explanation channels.

{{/if}}

Final thoughts

The best Spanish grammar books are tools, and like any tool they only work when you use them often. Pick one explanation book and one workbook for your level, spend ten minutes a day with them, and combine them with real reading and listening. Grammar will stop feeling like rules and start feeling like Spanish.

faq.q: What is the best Spanish grammar book for beginners?
faq.a: Complete Spanish Step-by-Step explains grammar clearly and in a logical order, with exercises. Easy Spanish Step-by-Step is a lighter alternative.

faq.q: What is the best Spanish grammar workbook?
faq.a: Practice Makes Perfect: Complete Spanish Grammar, for its large number of exercises and answer key.

faq.q: Is there a good Spanish grammar book written in Spanish?
faq.a: Gramática de uso del español, which comes in three levels from A1 to C2.

faq.q: What is the best Spanish grammar reference book?
faq.a: A New Reference Grammar of Modern Spanish by John Butt and Carmen Benjamin, for advanced learners and translators.

faq.q: Do I need a verb book to learn Spanish?
faq.a: It helps. 501 Spanish Verbs shows every tense of a verb on one page, which is useful at every level.
